name: Rise and Fall of the Delhi Sultanate

scenes.animation: Zippy is doing a jigsaw map of India, but every time he finishes, the pieces shuffle and rearrange themselves. A title card reads '11th to 17th centuries'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, this map of India keeps changing shape! Is it broken?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No, that is history. From the 11th century onward, invasions and new dynasties kept reshaping India's political map.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: We study this past to understand it, not to blame anyone living today.

scenes.animation: A timeline bar builds from left to right: '1192: Prithviraj Chauhan defeated', then '1206: Delhi Sultanate established'. Five blocks stack on top: 'Mamluks (Slave dynasty)', 'Khiljis', 'Tughlaqs', 'Sayyids', 'Lodis'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Invaders from beyond the Hindu Kush, many of them Turkic or Afghan, came for India's riches, for territory, and often to spread their religion by force.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After King Prithviraj Chauhan was defeated in 1192, the Delhi Sultanate was formed. The timeline marks 1206 for its establishment.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Five dynasties ruled it: the Mamluks, the Khiljis, the Tughlaqs, the Sayyids and the Lodis.

scenes.animation: A coin spins and stops, showing 'Sikander Sani, the second Alexander'. Arrows sweep from Delhi across north and central India and then southward, while Mongol horsemen at the northwest border are pushed back.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Around 1300, Ala-ud-din Khilji campaigned across north and central India, sacking many cities. He also repelled several Mongol invasions.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: His general Malik Kafur pushed south and attacked centres like Srirangam, Madurai and Chidambaram. The plunder paid for a huge army.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Successions were often violent. A sultan's average reign was hardly more than nine years.

scenes.animation: A map arrow stretches over 1,000 km from Delhi to Daulatabad and snaps back again, with tired travellers trudging along it. Then copper coins pile up next to a silver coin, and counterfeit copies multiply until a market scale tips over.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Who tried to move the whole capital?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Muhammad bin Tughlaq. For the first time since the Mauryas, most of the Subcontinent was under one ruler, but only briefly.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He moved his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad, then called Devagiri, forcing people to travel over 1,000 kilometres, and later moved it back.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: His token currency made copper coins worth silver or gold. People forged copper coins, and the economy declined.

scenes.animation: A dated tag '1398: Timur attacks Delhi' pins onto the timeline and the city skyline turns to smoke. Then a map shrinks the Sultanate from the large Tughlaq extent of 1335 to the small Lodi extent of 1479.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Some sultans imposed the jizya, a tax on non-Muslim subjects that was often a burden and a humiliation.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1398, Timur, a Turkic-Mongol conqueror, devastated Delhi and left with huge plunder.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Lodis became the last dynasty, but by then the Sultanate had shrunk a lot.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: remember the five Sultanate dynasties in order: Mamluk, Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a small Qutub Minar icon. Points appear: '1. 1206: Delhi Sultanate, five dynasties', '2. Khilji campaigns; Tughlaq's capital shift and token currency', '3. 1398 Timur; shrinking Lodi Sultanate'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: the Delhi Sultanate was established in 1206 and ruled by five Turkic-Afghan dynasties.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Ala-ud-din Khilji expanded it by force, and Muhammad bin Tughlaq's bold schemes were poorly executed.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: after Timur's attack in 1398, the Sultanate shrank until the Lodis.

name: Resistance to the Sultanate and the Vijayanagara Empire

scenes.animation: At Hampi, a tiny hare suddenly turns and chases a pack of surprised hounds. Zippy cheers from a rock as two brothers watch in amazement.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A hare chasing hounds? That is backwards!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Folklore says Harihara and Bukka saw exactly this. Their guru Vidyaranya called it a sign of courage and told them to build a capital there.

scenes.animation: A map of India lights up regions one by one: the Eastern Ganga kingdom of Kalinga in the east with the Konark Sun temple, Warangal in present-day Telangana, the Hoysala lands in present-day Karnataka with Belur and Halebidu, and Mewar in Rajasthan with Kumbhalgarh Fort's long wall.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Many kingdoms resisted the Sultanate. The Eastern Ganga ruler Narasimhadeva the First repelled its attacks and built the Surya temple at Konark.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Musunuri Nayakas united over 75 chieftains and drove Tughlaq's army out of Warangal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Hoysalas, builders of Belur and Halebidu, fended off attacks for a long time. In Mewar, Rana Kumbha built Kumbhalgarh Fort with its 36-kilometre wall.

scenes.animation: A timeline builds: '1336: Vijayanagara Empire', '1347: Bahmani Sultanate'. On a Deccan map, the Bahmani region splits into five labelled pieces: Bijapur, Golconda, Berar, Ahmednagar and Bidar.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the 14th century, Harihara and Bukka Raya, once governors under Muhammad bin Tughlaq, rejected Delhi's authority and founded what became the Vijayanagara Empire.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: To its north rose the Bahmani Sultanate, which later split into five Deccan Sultanates: Bijapur, Golconda, Berar, Ahmednagar and Bidar.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And kings called themselves pati, like Gajapati?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. Pati means lord. Vijayanagara kings were Narapati, and the Gajapatis ruled Odisha.

scenes.animation: Krishnadevaraya sits among poets holding scrolls in Sanskrit, Telugu and Kannada. The camera pans across the Vitthala temple, where Zippy taps a stone pillar and musical notes float out.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the 16th century, the empire peaked under Krishnadevaraya. He patronised poets and himself wrote a Telugu epic, Amuktamalyada.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He gave grants to temples like Tirupati and the Vitthala temple, famous for its musical pillars.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes wrote that the city seemed as large as Rome and was the best provided city in the world.

scenes.animation: A timeline pin drops at '1529: Krishnadevaraya dies', then '1565: Battle of Talikota'. The city of Vijayanagara fades into the ruins of present-day Hampi, and the map breaks into small Nayaka regions.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1565, the Deccan Sultanates united and defeated Vijayanagara at the Battle of Talikota.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The capital was sacked for months and left in ruins. The empire broke into regions ruled by Nayakas and ended in the mid-17th century.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: do not mix up the dates. Vijayanagara was established in 1336 and its capital was destroyed after Talikota in 1565.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a musical-pillar icon. Points appear: '1. Resistance: Eastern Gangas, Nayakas, Hoysalas, Mewar', '2. 1336 Vijayanagara; peak under Krishnadevaraya', '3. 1565 Talikota: capital destroyed'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: the Sultanate faced strong resistance from the Eastern Gangas, the Nayakas, the Hoysalas and Mewar.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Vijayanagara, founded by Harihara and Bukka, peaked under Krishnadevaraya.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: after the Battle of Talikota in 1565, its capital was destroyed and the empire fragmented.

name: The Mughals: From Babur to Aurangzeb

scenes.animation: Zippy flips through a giant illustrated book titled 'Baburnama' and finds pages full of birds and fruit trees. He looks up puzzled at Neo.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A conqueror who wrote about birds and mangoes?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That is Babur. His memoir shows a curious, cultured mind, but also a ruthless conqueror. History is often like that: complicated.

scenes.animation: A timeline builds: '1526: First Battle of Panipat' with cannons firing, '1530: Babur dies', then a brief 'Sur Empire' block, then '1556: Second Battle of Panipat'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Babur, a descendant of Timur, defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 using gunpowder and field artillery. This ended the Delhi Sultanate and founded the Mughal Empire.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After Babur, his son Humayun struggled, and Sher Shah Suri set up the Sur Empire, which was short-lived.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Himu, a Suri commander, briefly ruled Delhi as Hemchandra Vikramaditya, but was defeated by Akbar at the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556.

scenes.animation: A map of India fills in the Mughal Empire under Akbar by 1605. Icons pop up: a fort labelled 'Chittorgarh', a handshake labelled 'Alliances', a crossed-out tax sheet labelled 'Jizya abolished', and a scroll 'Sulh-i-kul: peace with all'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Akbar became emperor at 13. His reign blended brutality and tolerance.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Early on, after besieging Chittorgarh fort for months, he ordered a massacre of civilians.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Later he used alliances, welcomed Rajput leaders into his court, abolished the jizya and promoted sulh-i-kul, or peace with all.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: At Fatehpur Sikri, he had the Mahabharata and Ramayana translated into Persian.

scenes.animation: The Taj Mahal rises at Agra, followed by Humayun's tomb and the Red Forts of Delhi and Agra, with miniature paintings framing the screen.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Who built the Taj Mahal?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Shah Jahan, Akbar's grandson. His time marked a peak of art and architecture, with miniature painting and calligraphy flourishing too.

scenes.animation: A timeline adds '1658: Aurangzeb crowned', then '1707: Aurangzeb dies'. The Mughal map stretches to its largest extent in the south, while a treasury chest beside it empties coin by coin.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Aurangzeb seized the throne through a violent succession and crowned himself in 1658.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Under him, the empire reached its greatest extent, but he spent his last 25 years fighting in the Deccan, draining the treasury.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: He reimposed the jizya and a pilgrimage tax, and ordered temples destroyed. After his death in 1707, Mughal power declined rapidly.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: a favourite question compares Akbar's methods with those of earlier rulers who relied mostly on military might.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a small Taj Mahal icon. Points appear: '1. 1526 Panipat: Babur founds Mughal Empire', '2. Akbar: conquest plus alliances and sulh-i-kul', '3. Aurangzeb: largest empire, then decline after 1707'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: Babur's victory at Panipat in 1526 founded the Mughal Empire.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Akbar combined conquest with alliances, abolished the jizya and promoted peace with all.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: Aurangzeb's empire was the largest, but long wars weakened it, and it declined after 1707.

scenes.animation: On the Brahmaputra, a huge fleet of big boats faces a smaller fleet of swift Ahom boats. Zippy, holding binoculars, counts '30,000 versus 10,000' on a scoreboard.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Ten thousand against thirty thousand? The small side has no chance!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Wait and see. Across India, many groups resisted Mughal power, and some won.

scenes.animation: A map of India lights up resistance points: Jat peasants in western Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and eastern Rajasthan; forest symbols for the Bhils, Gonds, Santhals and Kochs; and the Garha kingdom in central India with a portrait of Rani Durgavati and '1564'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Peasants rebelled against harsh exploitation. In the 17th century, Jat peasants rose up, though their rebellion was suppressed.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Tribal groups like the Bhils, Gonds, Santhals and Kochs fought attempts to take their land or tax them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Rani Durgavati of the Gond kingdom of Garha ruled wisely. When Akbar's general attacked in 1564, she fought bravely despite being outnumbered.

scenes.animation: The Aravalli hills rise on screen. A timeline pin reads '1576: Battle of Haldighati'. Maharana Pratap rides into the hills, joined by Bhil archers; the Mewar emblem appears with a Bhil warrior on it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Rajputs of Mewar and Marwar often resisted invaders. Rana Sanga united several clans but lost to Babur at Khanwa.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Maharana Pratap refused Mughal overlordship. At Haldighati in 1576 he was forced to retreat, but he fought on through guerrilla warfare from the Aravallis.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Bhils supported him as archers and guides, which is why a Bhil warrior appears on the Mewar emblem.

scenes.animation: Back on the Brahmaputra near Guwahati, a timeline pin reads '1671: Battle of Saraighat'. Lachit Borphukan leads the Ahom boats through narrow river channels and the large Mughal fleet turns back.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Ahoms came from present-day Myanmar in the 13th century. Under their paik system, every able-bodied man served the state in return for land rights.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1671, at the Battle of Saraighat, Lachit Borphukan and 10,000 men defeated a Mughal force of 30,000.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So the rivers and forests were their secret weapon!

scenes.animation: A timeline builds for Punjab: 'Guru Nanak, 15th century: Ik Onkar', '1675: Guru Tegh Bahadur martyred', '1699: Khalsa formed by Guru Gobind Singh', '1799: Sikh Empire'. Gurudwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Chandni Chowk glows softly.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Guru Nanak taught equality and the oneness of God. Later Gurus faced persecution, and Guru Hargobind formed a Sikh army.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In 1675, Guru Tegh Bahadur stood up for persecuted Kashmiri Pandits and was executed in Chandni Chowk on Aurangzeb's orders.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: His son Guru Gobind Singh formed the Khalsa in 1699. Later, Maharaja Ranjit Singh united the Sikhs into a strong empire.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: remember who led each resistance: Lachit Borphukan at Saraighat, Maharana Pratap at Haldighati, Rani Durgavati in Garha.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a boat and shield icon. Points appear: '1. Peasants, tribes and Rani Durgavati resisted', '2. Rajputs: Haldighati 1576; Ahoms: Saraighat 1671', '3. Sikhs: Khalsa 1699, Sikh Empire under Ranjit Singh'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: peasants, tribal groups and rulers like Rani Durgavati resisted Mughal expansion.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Maharana Pratap fought on after Haldighati, and the Ahoms won at Saraighat in 1671.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: the Sikhs formed the Khalsa in 1699 and later built a strong empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

scenes.animation: Zippy runs a pretend kingdom from a cushion throne, trying to collect taxes, lead the army and judge disputes all at once until he collapses in a heap of scrolls.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Running a kingdom is exhausting! How did the sultans manage?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: They had help. Let's see how both the Sultanate and the Mughals organised their rule.

scenes.animation: A flowchart builds: 'Sultan (absolute authority)' at the top, a 'Council of ministers' box beneath, and arrows to land blocks labelled 'Iqta' held by 'Iqtadars', with coins flowing up to a treasury and an army.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The sultan had absolute authority, helped by a council of ministers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Under the iqta system, nobles called iqtadars were assigned territories to collect taxes, mainly to maintain the army. These posts were not hereditary.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The heaviest burden fell on peasants.

scenes.animation: A second flowchart builds under the title 'Akbar's administration': 'Diwan: finance', 'Mir Bakhshi: military', 'Khan-i-Saman: public works, trade, royal household', 'Sadr: justice, religion, education'. Below, a map splits into '12 subahs', and a mansabdar stands beside a line of horses, elephants and camels.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Akbar had the Diwan for finance, the Mir Bakhshi for the military, the Khan-i-Saman for public works and the Sadr for justice. The empire had twelve provinces called subahs.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Under the mansabdari system, officers maintained a fixed number of troops and animals according to their rank. They were paid in land called jagirs.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Todar Mal, his finance minister, surveyed land, crop yields and prices to set revenue.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: do not confuse iqta with mansabdari. Iqta belongs to the Sultanate; mansabdari belongs to the Mughals.

scenes.animation: An outline map of India shows ports appearing: Surat, Calicut, Mangalore, Masulipatnam and Hooghly. Ships sail out with cotton and spices, while horses and silk arrive; a Persian wheel turns in a field.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Agriculture was the mainstay. Irrigation like the Persian wheel helped farmers grow rice, wheat, sugarcane, cotton and more.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Indian goods left through ports like Surat, Calicut and Hooghly. India exported far more than it imported.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: How did traders move money without getting robbed?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: With a hundi, a written payment instruction. It worked across borders, like an early form of banking.

scenes.animation: A temple courtyard bustles with a market, a water tank and a pilgrim rest house. Then the colours dim: a peasant hands most of his harvest to tax collectors, while neighbours of different faiths still trade at a village market.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Temples were economic hubs too, building tanks and rest houses and giving merchants credit.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: By the late 1600s, many peasants kept only a small share of their harvest, and wealth sat with rulers and elites.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yet, by and large, people of different faiths lived peacefully side by side, depending on each other.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a scroll and coin icon. Points appear: '1. Sultanate: sultan, ministers, iqta system', '2. Mughals: ministers, subahs, mansabdari, Todar Mal', '3. Rich trade and hundi; hardship for common people; resilience'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One: the Sultanate ran on the sultan, a council of ministers and the iqta system.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: Akbar organised ministers, subahs, the mansabdari system and Todar Mal's revenue surveys.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: trade flourished, but common people often struggled, and Indian society stayed resilient.
